An organizing principle in the study of the Jacobian Conjecture

Frederico Xavier
Abstract

Let Ω\Omega be an irreducible component of the locus of polynomial maps F:ℂn→ℂnF:\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} satisfying deg​F≤k\text{\rm deg}F\leq k and det​D​F=1\text{det}DF=1. It is shown that either Ω⊂Aut​(ℂn)\Omega\subset\text{\rm Aut}(\mathbb{C}^{n}), as claimed by the Jacobian Conjecture, or the general F∈ΩF\in\Omega is not an automorphism.

1 Introduction

The Jacobian Conjecture (JC) claims that every polynomial map F:ℂn→ℂnF:\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} satisfying det​D​F=1\text{det}DF=1 is invertible [1, 2]. Let 𝒫nk\mathcal{P}_{n}^{k} be the vector space of all polynomial maps F=(F1,…,Fn):ℂn→ℂnF=(F_{1},\dots,F_{n}):\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} with deg​F=defmax⁡deg​Fj≤k,\text{\rm deg}F\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\max\text{\rm deg}F_{j}\leq k, and Vnk⊂𝒫nkV_{n}^{k}\subset\mathcal{P}_{n}^{k} the algebraic locus given by det​D​F=1\text{\rm det}DF=1. In this notation JC is the claim that ⋃n,k∈ℕVnk⊂Aut​(ℂn)\bigcup_{n,k\in\mathbb{N}}V_{n}^{k}\subset\text{Aut}(\mathbb{C}^{n}). Our goal is to investigate JC at the finer level of a fixed irreducible component Ω\Omega of VnkV_{n}^{k}.

Theorem 1.1.

Either every F∈ΩF\in\Omega is invertible or the general F∈ΩF\in\Omega is non-invertible. Thus, either JC holds in Ω\Omega or almost every F∈ΩF\in\Omega is actually a counterexample of JC.

As injective polynomial maps ℂn→ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} are bijective (the Ax-Grothendieck theorem), one obtains the following probabilistic criterion to resolve the ambiguity in the dichotomy: Almost surely, the correct alternative in Thm.1.1 is the first one if and only if for a random choice of (F,c)∈Ω×ℂn(F,c)\in\Omega\times\mathbb{C}^{n} the solution of F⁡(z)=cF(z)=c in ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} exists and is unique.

JC has been verified for several classes of maps with special properties (e.g. quadratic maps [3]), but all attempts at establishing it in full generality were found to be faulty. The fact that Thm.1.1 is a dichotomy puts this history in perspective and opens up the possibility that maybe JC fails for some pair (Vnk,Ω)(V_{n}^{k},\Omega). It is conceivable that an application of the above criterion to all components of all VnkV_{n}^{k} may lead to counterexamples. The silver lining in such a difficult task is that one only needs for the algorithm to reach the conjectural “right”Ω\Omega, as the counterexamples would then be nearly “impossible”to miss.

2 Proof of Theorem 1.1

Because there is a wider audience for the Jacobian Conjecture, the conceptual presentation that follows contains more details than it is usually the case in research papers. We begin by fixing notation and terminology. Let N⁡(n,k)N(n,k) be the dimension of the complex vector space of polynomials in z1,…,znz_{1},\dots,z_{n} that have degree at most kk, so that dim​𝒫nk=n​N​(n,k)\text{dim}\;\mathcal{P}_{n}^{k}=nN(n,k). A subset CC of 𝒫nk\mathcal{P}_{n}^{k} is called algebraic if, for some (and hence every) linear isomorphism Λ:ℂn​N​(n,k)→𝒫nk\Lambda:\mathbb{C}^{nN(n,k)}\to\mathcal{P}_{n}^{k}, Λ−1​(C)\Lambda^{-1}(C) is algebraic in the affine sense, i.e. Λ−1​(C)\Lambda^{-1}(C) is the intersection of zero sets of polynomials.

If we assume that the nonempty set Ink=defVnk∩Aut​(ℂn)I_{n}^{k}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}V_{n}^{k}\cap\text{Aut}(\mathbb{C}^{n}) is algebraic in 𝒫nk\mathcal{P}_{n}^{k} then the theorem follows in a straightforward way. Indeed, if Ω∩Ink=∅\Omega\cap I_{n}^{k}=\emptyset the second alternative in Thm.1.1 holds in the stronger sense that all maps in Ω\Omega are non-invertible. Otherwise, Ω∩Ink⊂Ω\Omega\cap I_{n}^{k}\subset\Omega is an inclusion of non-empty algebraic sets. If Ω∩Ink=Ω\Omega\cap I_{n}^{k}=\Omega, the first alternative holds. If ∅≠Ω∩Ink≠Ω\emptyset\neq\Omega\cap I_{n}^{k}\neq\Omega, the irreducibility of Ω\Omega implies the inequality dim​(Ω∩Ink)<dim​Ω\text{dim}(\Omega\cap I_{n}^{k})<\text{dim}\Omega. In this case the second alternative holds, where the relevant non-empty Zariski open (hence dense) subset of Ω\Omega where the general maps live is Ω−(Ω∩Ink)\Omega-(\Omega\cap I_{n}^{k}).

The proof that InkI_{n}^{k} is algebraic in 𝒫nk\mathcal{P}_{n}^{k} will be the object of the remainder of this note. To implement analytic arguments it is convenient to work with the isomorphism Λ=Λnk\Lambda=\Lambda_{n}^{k} described below. Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be the set of polynomials z1α1​…​znαnz_{1}^{\alpha_{1}}\dots z_{n}^{\alpha_{n}}, αj≥0\alpha_{j}\geq 0, α1+⋯+αn≤k\alpha_{1}+\dots+\alpha_{n}\leq k, endowed with some order. The cardinality of ℬ\mathcal{B} is of course N⁡(n,k)N(n,k). Define an isomorphism Λnk:ℂn​N​(n,k)→𝒫nk\Lambda_{n}^{k}:\mathbb{C}^{nN(n,k)}\to\mathcal{P}_{n}^{k} as follows. Multiply each of the first N⁡(n,k)N(n,k) coordinates of c∈ℂn​N​(n,k)c\in\mathbb{C}^{nN(n,k)} by the respective polynomial in ℬ\mathcal{B}, and then add all terms. The resulting polynomial is, by definition, the first component of Λnk​c\Lambda_{n}^{k}c. Similarly, using the second block of N⁡(n,k)N(n,k) coordinates of cc, re-indexed from 11 to N⁡(n,k)N(n,k), multiply each coordinate by the corresponding polynomial in ℬ\mathcal{B} and add all terms to produce the second component of Λnk​c\Lambda_{n}^{k}c. Proceed in this fashion, up to the re-indexed nn-th block of N⁡(n,k)N(n,k) coordinates of cc, to define all components of Λnk​c\Lambda_{n}^{k}c. For any given F∈𝒫nkF\in\mathcal{P}_{n}^{k} the vector (Λnk)−1​F(\Lambda_{n}^{k})^{-1}F is simply an ordered list of the coefficients of all components FiF_{i} of FF.

The set (Λnk)−1​Vnk(\Lambda_{n}^{k})^{-1}V_{n}^{k} is obviously Zariski-closed, since it is defined by the polynomial relations among the coefficients of all FiF_{i} that arise by setting det​D​F​(z)=1,z∈ℂn\text{det}DF(z)=1,\;z\in\mathbb{C}^{n}.

To prove the theorem we must argue that (Λnk)−1​Ink(\Lambda_{n}^{k})^{-1}I_{n}^{k} is also Zariski-closed. In order to do this, consider the set

Tj=def{(c,z,w)∈ℂn​N​(n,k)×ℂn×ℂn)|Λnkc(z)−Λnkc(w)=0,zj−wj≠0},T_{j}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\big\{(c,z,w)\in\mathbb{C}^{nN(n,k)}\times\mathbb{C}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}^{n})\;|\;\Lambda_{n}^{k}c(z)-\Lambda_{n}^{k}c(w)=0,\;z_{j}-w_{j}\neq 0\big\},

where 1≤j≤n1\leq j\leq n, z=(z1,…,zn),w=(w1,…,wn).z=(z_{1},\dots,z_{n}),w=(w_{1},\dots,w_{n}). Relative to the Zariski topology of ℂn​N​(n,k)+2​n≈ℂn​N​(n,k)×ℂn×ℂn\mathbb{C}^{nN(n,k)+2n}\approx\mathbb{C}^{nN(n,k)}\times\mathbb{C}^{n}\times\mathbb{C}^{n}, TjT_{j} is the intersection of a closed set and an open one. Hence, the set T=T1∪⋯∪TnT=T_{1}\cup\dots\cup T_{n} is constructible. By a special case of Chevalley’s theorem, the projection π1​(T)⊂ℂn​N​(n,k)\pi_{1}(T)\subset\mathbb{C}^{nN(n,k)} is also constructible. Manifestly, an element of π1​(T)\pi_{1}(T) is a list of the coefficients of a non-injective map in 𝒫nk\mathcal{P}_{n}^{k}. Conversely, any such map arises in this way.

Since the class of constructible sets is invariant under the operations of taking complements and finite intersections, (ℂn​N​(n,k)−π1​(T))∩(Λnk)−1​Vnk(\mathbb{C}^{nN(n,k)}-\pi_{1}(T))\cap(\Lambda_{n}^{k})^{-1}V_{n}^{k} is also constructible. Clearly, an element of this set is a list of the coefficients of some injective polynomial map that belongs to VnkV_{n}^{k} (and conversely). By the Ax-Grothendieck theorem one concludes that (Λnk)−1​Ink=(ℂn​N​(n,k)−π1​(T))∩(Λnk)−1​Vnk.(\Lambda_{n}^{k})^{-1}I_{n}^{k}=(\mathbb{C}^{nN(n,k)}-\pi_{1}(T))\cap(\Lambda_{n}^{k})^{-1}V_{n}^{k}. It follows from this equality and the previous discussion that (Λnk)−1​Ink(\Lambda_{n}^{k})^{-1}I_{n}^{k} is constructible. To finish the proof of Thm.1.1 we must improve matters and argue that (Λnk)−1​Ink(\Lambda_{n}^{k})^{-1}I_{n}^{k} is actually Zariski-closed. Since the Euclidean and Zariski closures of a constructible set are equal, it suffices to prove that (Λnk)−1​Ink(\Lambda_{n}^{k})^{-1}I_{n}^{k} is classically closed.

From this point on the arguments are analytic and topological. Consider a sequence (c(j))(c^{(j)}) in ℂn​N​(n,k)\mathbb{C}^{nN(n,k)}, j∈ℕj\in\mathbb{N}, satisfying the following conditions:

i) c(j)⟶j→∞c∈ℂn​N​(n,k)c^{(j)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle j\to\infty}}{{\longrightarrow}}c\in\mathbb{C}^{nN(n,k)}.
ii) det​D​Λnk​c(j)​(z)=1,z∈ℂn\text{\rm det}D\Lambda_{n}^{k}{c^{(j)}}(z)=1,z\in\mathbb{C}^{n}.
iii) Λnk​c(j):ℂn→ℂn\Lambda_{n}^{k}{c^{(j)}}:\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} is injective.

As observed before, the injective maps in 𝒫nk\mathcal{P}_{n}^{k} are invertible. Conditions ii) and iii), taken together, are then equivalent to c(j)∈(Λnk)−1​Inkc^{(j)}\in(\Lambda_{n}^{k})^{-1}I_{n}^{k}. Since our immediate goal is to show that (Λnk)−1​Ink(\Lambda_{n}^{k})^{-1}I_{n}^{k} is closed in the Euclidean topology, we must argue that c∈(Λnk)−1​Inkc\in(\Lambda_{n}^{k})^{-1}I_{n}^{k} as well, i.e. that ii) and iii) still hold if c(j)c^{(j)} is replaced by cc. Regarding ii), continuity and i) imply det​D​Λnk​c​(z)=1\text{\rm det}D\Lambda_{n}^{k}{c}(z)=1. The analysis of the analogue of iii) is a bit more involved. Since det​D​Λnk​c​(z)\text{\rm det}D\Lambda_{n}^{k}{c}(z) is nowhere zero, the complex inverse function theorem implies that Λnk​c:ℂn→ℂn\Lambda_{n}^{k}c:\mathbb{C}^{n}\to\mathbb{C}^{n} has local analytic (hence continuous) inverses, and so its realification G=defΛnk​c~:ℝ2​n→ℝ2​n,G\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\widetilde{\Lambda_{n}^{k}c}:\mathbb{R}^{2n}\to\mathbb{R}^{2n}, obtained by taking real and imaginary parts of the components of Λnk​c\Lambda_{n}^{k}{c}, is a local homeomorphism.

Next, we need a topological observation:

(†\dagger) If (Gj)(G_{j}) is a sequence of injective local homeomorphisms Gj:ℝm→ℝmG_{j}:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}^{m} that converges locally uniformly to a local homeomorphism G:ℝm→ℝmG:\mathbb{R}^{m}\to\mathbb{R}^{m}, then GG is also injective.

(In passing, elementary one-dimensional examples show that the analogue of (†\dagger) fails if injectivity is replaced by surjectivity.) For completeness, we provide the arguments for (†\dagger). Assume by contradiction that G⁡(p1)=G⁡(p2)=qG(p_{1})=G(p_{2})=q, with p1≠p2p_{1}\neq p_{2}, and let U1,U2U_{1},U_{2} be disjoint bounded neighborhoods of p1p_{1} and p2p_{2} whose closures are mapped homeomorphically by GG onto a neighborhood WW of qq. As q∉G⁡(∂Ui)q\notin G(\partial U_{i}) for i=1,2i=1,2, the topological degree d⁡(G,Ui,q)d(G,U_{i},q) is defined and has value ±1\pm 1 because Ui¯→GW\overline{U_{i}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle G}}{{\to}}W is a homeomorphism. Since Gj|Ui¯⟶j→∞G|Ui¯G_{j}|{\overline{U_{i}}}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle j\to\infty}}{{\longrightarrow}}G|\overline{U_{i}} uniformly, d⁡(Gj,Ui,q)d(G_{j},U_{i},q) is also defined for all sufficiently large jj and d⁡(Gj,Ui,q)=d⁡(G,Ui,q)≠0.d(G_{j},U_{i},q)=d(G,U_{i},q)\neq 0. In particular, Gj​(x)=qG_{j}(x)=q has solutions in both disjoint sets U1U_{1} and U2U_{2}, a contradiction to the injectivity of GjG_{j}.

∎

It is easy to see that for any given compact set K⊂ℂnK\subset\mathbb{C}^{n} there exists a constant C⁡(n,k,K)C(n,k,K), independent of jj, such that

supz∈K‖Λnk​c(j)​(z)−Λnk​c​(z)‖=supz∈K‖Λnk​(c(j)−c)​(z)‖≤C⁡(n,k,K)​‖c(j)−c‖.\displaystyle\sup_{z\in K}||\Lambda_{n}^{k}c^{(j)}(z)-\Lambda_{n}^{k}c(z)||=\sup_{z\in K}||\Lambda_{n}^{k}(c^{(j)}-c)(z)||\leq C(n,k,K)||c^{(j)}-c||. (2.1)

A consequence of i) and (2.1) is that Λnk​c(j)⟶j→∞Λnk​c\Lambda_{n}^{k}c^{(j)}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle j\to\infty}}{{\longrightarrow}}\Lambda_{n}^{k}c locally uniformly. In particular, the induced injective local homeomorphisms Gj=defΛnk​c(j)~:ℝ2​n→ℝ2​nG_{j}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\widetilde{\Lambda_{n}^{k}c^{(j)}}:\mathbb{R}^{2n}\to\mathbb{R}^{2n} converge locally uniformly to the local homeomorphism G=defΛnk​c~G\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\text{def}}}{{=}}\widetilde{\Lambda_{n}^{k}c}. It follows from (†\dagger) that Λnk​c~\widetilde{\Lambda_{n}^{k}c} is injective, and evidently so is Λnk​c{\Lambda_{n}^{k}c}. Thus, the analogue of iii) with cc replacing c(j)c^{(j)} holds, and (Λnk)−1​Ink(\Lambda_{n}^{k})^{-1}I_{n}^{k} is classically closed, completing the proof of the theorem.

3 Related results

Regarding the problem in real algebraic geometry of understanding when a polynomial map G:ℝn→ℝnG:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}^{n} can be inverted, in [5] we use ideas from nonlinear optimization and the Tarski-Seidenberg theorem to establish the existence of a subset ker​(G)\text{\rm ker}(G) of ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} satisfying:

i) ker​(G)\text{\rm ker}(G) is semialgebraic.

ii) 0∈ker​(G)0\in\text{\rm ker}(G) and ker​(G)={0}\text{\rm ker}(G)=\{0\} if and only if GG is invertible.

iii) If GG is linear then ker​(G)\text{\rm ker}(G) is the usual kernel.

An earlier version of these results, valid for polynomial local diffeomorphisms, can be found in [4]. For analytic, topological, and geometric mechanisms of global inversion of maps in the smooth category, we refer to the semi-expository paper [6] and the references therein.
